source.title: Binary Classification of Gaussian Mixtures: Abundance of Support Vectors, Benign Overfitting, and Regularization

record.tranche_reason: The study extends benign-overfitting analysis to overparameterized linear classifiers on Gaussian-mixture data, including a probabilistic label-noise model. Its results concern linear models, not the deep networks named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study's own results cover linear classification, not neural networks. It does not test completely random labels, unstructured inputs, training-time ratios, regularization effects on fitting random labels, or learning order. Background statements about deep networks and results cited from other papers are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study proves results for linear SVM and least-squares classifiers on Gaussian-mixture data. All six versions concern deep networks. Its restricted label-flip model also does not test completely random labels or a corruption sweep to chance. These related theoretical results do not test any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's main paraphrase is accurate: sufficient overparameterization, covariance structure, and signal conditions permit interpolating linear classifiers to generalize well, including under restricted probabilistic label corruption. The authors also identify covariance-dependent regimes where unregularized interpolation outperforms ridge regularization. These conclusions do not establish any listed deep-network version.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes linear SVM and min-norm least-squares classifiers on synthetic Gaussian-mixture data; it does not reproduce neural-network training on image datasets with random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Theoretical outcomes depend on covariance structure, signal-to-noise ratio, overparameterization, and, in the noisy model, the corruption setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Under sufficient overparameterization and signal conditions, linear SVM and minimum-norm LS coincide and interpolate independently corrupted labels. In the restricted isotropic noisy model, their noisy-distribution risk approaches γ under additional scaling conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterized linear classifiers can interpolate partially corrupted Gaussian-mixture labels while approaching the noisy-distribution error floor.

fits_no_version.finding: In Figure 3's noiseless Gaussian-mixture setting, LS and SVM errors decrease toward zero as dimension increases, and all training points eventually become support vectors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear classifiers can generalize well while interpolating sufficiently high-dimensional Gaussian-mixture data.

record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The results are for synthetic Gaussian-mixture models and linear classifiers, so they do not directly test the deep-network claim. Several simulation results are figure-only; exact plotted values are not stated in the text. The noisy model assumes independent label flips with corruption probability bounded by 1/C for a large constant.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying deep-network or image-labeling outcomes are reported. Background claims and cited results are excluded. Other regularization simulations and theoretical bounds do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: Deep-network fitting of completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios and convergence changes with increasing label corruption.
Deep-network fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect deep-network training fit across a corruption sweep and steady test-error degradation toward chance.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on deep-network random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions because every row concerns a different system or measure; they do not indicate that the paper's linear-model results failed. Gaussian feature noise around class-dependent means is not the unstructured Gaussian-noise input experiment in V3.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels and deep networks.
Relative training time and convergence as corruption increases.
Deep networks; a sweep from no corruption to fully random labels; steady test-error degradation toward chance.
Weight decay, dropout and data augmentation effects on random-label fitting and true-label generalization in deep networks.
Whether deep networks learn real-label patterns before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: noisy GMM with Σ = I; SVM solution
rows.size_stated: n training samples; feature dimension p
rows.operation_detail: Fit SVM using corrupted labels in the noisy Gaussian-mixture model.

conditions.value: corruption probability γ; 0 ≤ γ ≤ 1/C for a large constant C
p > C1 n log n + n − 1 and p > C2 max{n log(2n)‖η‖2, n‖η‖²2}

rows.measure: Whether the SVM solution linearly interpolates the observed corrupted labels.
rows.value: linear interpolation with probability at least (1 − C3/n)
rows.note: The result is a theorem for linear classifiers and probabilistic label flips, not a test of completely random labels or neural networks.
rows.check: Interpolation is established for linear SVM, not deep networks. Theorem 6 requires n√log(2n)‖η‖₂ in the second dimensional condition; the record omits the square root. The theorem's interpolation result itself is correctly reported.

rows.subject: noisy GMM with Σ = I; min-norm LS estimator
rows.size_stated: n training samples; feature dimension p
rows.operation_detail: Fit the min-norm interpolating LS estimator using corrupted labels.

conditions.value: conditions in (21); p > b·n; (1 − n/p)‖η‖2 > C

rows.measure: Expected 0–1 classification risk on the clean-label distribution.
rows.note: This is a bound for a linear estimator in a fixed probabilistic-noise setting; the paper does not report a corruption-fraction sweep.
rows.check: The linear-estimator risk bound measures no listed version. Calling its outcome clean-label risk is misleading: Section 7 interprets γ as an unavoidable test-label corruption floor. Clean-label error does not have an unavoidable γ floor. Record the noisy-distribution risk bound and retain its distinction from a measured error.

rows.subject: noisy GMM with Σ = I; SVM solution
rows.size_stated: n training samples; feature dimension p
rows.operation_detail: Fit SVM using corrupted labels under the conditions of Theorem 7.

conditions.value: p/n → ∞; p > max{C2 n log n + n − 1, C3 n log(2n)‖η‖2, n‖η‖²2}; ‖η‖⁴2 ≥ C4(p/n)^α, α > 1

rows.measure: Classification error on the clean-label distribution and interpolation of corrupted training labels.
rows.value: classification error approaches γ; SVM linearly interpolates the data
rows.note: The theorem states asymptotic behavior for the specified noisy GMM regime; it does not establish smooth degradation over a range of corruption levels.
rows.check: The result concerns linear SVM. Corollary 7.1 describes risk approaching γ under the noisy model, not clean-label error approaching γ. Its dimensional condition contains n√log(2n)‖η‖₂, rather than n log(2n)‖η‖₂.

rows.subject: GMM; LS estimates and SVM solutions
rows.operation_detail: Fit LS and SVM classifiers on noiseless Gaussian-mixture data and measure classification error.
rows.measure: Classification error as a function of p.
rows.uncertainty: averages over 300 Monte-Carlo realizations (simulation protocol stated in Section 3)
rows.note: The text describes the error as decreasing toward zero as p increases, but the plotted values are not transcribed. The finding concerns linear classifiers on true-label GMM data.
rows.check: True-label generalization of linear classifiers measures no listed version. Although exact plotted values are unavailable, Section 5 explicitly establishes the qualitative finding that error decreases toward zero; the outcome is not wholly unreadable.

rows.subject: GMM; SVM solutions
rows.operation_detail: Measure the proportion of training points that are SVM support vectors.
rows.uncertainty: averages over 300 Monte-Carlo realizations (simulation protocol stated in Section 3)
rows.note: The authors state that all data points become support vectors for sufficiently large p; precise plotted values are not given in text.
rows.check: Support-vector fraction measures no listed version. Section 5 explicitly reports that all training points become support vectors for sufficiently large p, although exact intermediate plotted fractions are unavailable.

rows.subject: GMM; min-norm LS estimator
rows.size_stated: n training samples; feature dimension p
rows.operation_detail: Fit the min-norm LS estimator on noisy GMM data with corrupted labels.

conditions.value: probabilistic label flips with corruption probability γ

rows.measure: Whether the estimator interpolates the observed corrupted labels.
rows.value: The regime is one where η̂LS = η̂SVM; both interpolate the data under the stated conditions.
rows.note: The study defines the noisy model with independently flipped labels, but γ is restricted to be at most 1/C for a large constant.
rows.check: This is a consequence of the same SVM–LS equivalence recorded in R1, not an independent outcome. LS interpolation is imposed by its defining optimization constraint. Neither result establishes random-label fitting by deep networks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
